title: Learn Pub/Sub in RabbitMQ and Go
description: Build event-driven Go services with queues, exchanges, routing, and delivery guarantees.

lessons.title: Learn Pub/Sub Architecture
lessons.instruction: A publisher emits an event without knowing which subscribers will handle it. The broker routes the event, allowing subscribers to evolve independently. Publish the user.created event so the matching handler runs.

lessons.title: Publisher
lessons.instruction: A RabbitMQ publisher sends a body to an exchange with a routing key; it does not address a consumer directly. Publish the order event with the routing key expected by downstream bindings.

lessons.title: Subscriber
lessons.instruction: A subscriber processes deliveries selected by its queue bindings. Handle the orders.created delivery and ignore unrelated topics.

lessons.title: Event-Driven Design
lessons.instruction: One event can fan out to independent reactions, but that decoupling also introduces eventual consistency and retry concerns. Register both reactions without making either handler call the other.

lessons.title: RabbitMQ
lessons.instruction: RabbitMQ is the broker used by this course. Run Check to verify that its management endpoint is responding before you build publishers and consumers.
lessons.starter: check
lessons.expected: PASS · The live pubsub services are ready.

lessons.title: Alternative Brokers
lessons.instruction: RabbitMQ excels at queueing and flexible routing, Kafka at durable replayable logs, and NATS at lightweight low-latency messaging. Complete the chooser so each workload gets the intended broker.

lessons.title: Connect
lessons.instruction: An AMQP connection is long-lived, while channels are lighter logical sessions created from it. Open a channel and close it before the connection when main returns.

lessons.title: AMQP Protocol
lessons.instruction: AMQP separates routing metadata from message content. Fill the envelope with an exchange, routing key, content type, and body like a publisher would send.

lessons.title: MQTT and STOMP
lessons.instruction: MQTT is compact topic-based messaging for constrained clients; STOMP uses simple text frames; AMQP exposes richer broker semantics. Return the protocol that matches each client need.

lessons.title: Exchanges and Queues
lessons.instruction: Publishers send to exchanges; bindings decide which queues receive a message; consumers read from queues. Use the binding key that routes this email job into the jobs queue.

lessons.title: Types of Exchanges
lessons.instruction: Direct exchanges match exact keys, fanout exchanges ignore keys, topic exchanges match dot-delimited patterns, and headers exchanges inspect metadata. Implement those four routing decisions.

lessons.title: Create a Queue
lessons.instruction: Queue declaration is idempotent only when the existing queue has the same properties. Make both declarations agree so a second declaration succeeds.

lessons.title: Transient Queues
lessons.instruction: A private temporary subscriber commonly uses a server-generated, non-durable, exclusive, auto-delete queue. Configure those lifecycle properties.

lessons.title: Decoupling
lessons.instruction: A service can depend on an event contract and a publisher interface instead of a concrete downstream service. Emit user.created through the provided publisher.

lessons.title: Client REPL
lessons.instruction: A small publisher REPL should parse a command, reject malformed input, and preserve a multi-word body. Correct the command verb so it prints the parsed topic and body.

lessons.title: Sync vs. Async
lessons.instruction: An unbuffered channel models a synchronous handoff; a buffer allows producers to enqueue limited work without waiting for an immediate receiver. Give the asynchronous path room for three events.
lessons.starter:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	syncEvents := make(chan int)
	asyncEvents := make(chan int)
	fmt.Printf("sync=%d async=%d\n", cap(syncEvents), cap(asyncEvents))
}
lessons.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	syncEvents := make(chan int)
	asyncEvents := make(chan int, 3)
	fmt.Printf("sync=%d async=%d\n", cap(syncEvents), cap(asyncEvents))
}

lessons.title: Topic Exchange
lessons.instruction: Topic bindings use dot-delimited words: * matches exactly one word and # matches zero or more. Implement matching for the supplied bindings and routing keys.

lessons.title: Durable
lessons.instruction: A durable exchange, durable queue, and persistent message are separate settings. Enable all three; one setting alone does not make the complete route survive a broker restart.

lessons.title: Consumers
lessons.instruction: A Go consumer commonly ranges over a delivery channel until it closes. Send both deliveries before closing the channel so the loop drains them cleanly.

lessons.title: Multi Consumers
lessons.instruction: Consumers sharing one queue compete for work: each delivery goes to one consumer rather than every consumer. Distribute the jobs round-robin across two workers.
lessons.expected:
consumer-1 job-1
consumer-2 job-2
consumer-1 job-3
consumer-2 job-4

lessons.title: Routing Patterns
lessons.instruction: Bindings describe subscription intent, and overlapping bindings can route one publication to multiple queues. Publish the order.created key and print the matching queues in stable order.

lessons.title: Naming
lessons.instruction: Shared durable queues need stable semantic names; private exclusive queues can use server-generated names. Return the appropriate name for each lifecycle.

lessons.title: Dead Letter
lessons.instruction: RabbitMQ can dead-letter messages that are rejected without requeue, expire, or exceed a queue limit. Mark the broker-managed dead-letter reasons without treating shutdown as one.

lessons.title: Ack and Nack
lessons.instruction: Ack removes a successfully processed delivery. Nack can requeue a transient failure or discard a permanent failure. Return the settlement that matches each handler result.

lessons.title: Dead Letter Queue
lessons.instruction: A dead-letter exchange routes failed messages; a dead-letter queue is a queue bound to it. Preserve the original routing key and failure reason so operators can diagnose the message.

lessons.title: Exact Delivery
lessons.instruction: A broker commonly provides at-most-once or at-least-once delivery, not end-to-end exactly-once effects. Make the consumer idempotent by recording message IDs and skipping a duplicate.
lessons.expected:
handled m1
skipped m1
handled m2

lessons.title: Nack Requeue
lessons.instruction: Requeue failures that may succeed later, dead-letter permanently invalid messages, and acknowledge successful work. Correct the policy for invalid payloads.

lessons.title: Nack Requeue Fix
lessons.instruction: Requeueing a poison message forever creates a hot failure loop. Allow two retries, then dead-letter the third failed attempt.

lessons.title: Data Serialization
lessons.instruction: RabbitMQ carries bytes, so producers and consumers need an agreed content type and payload shape. Encode a versioned JSON event with explicit fields.

lessons.title: Game Logs
lessons.instruction: Structured game events should carry stable fields such as event type, timestamp, player, and outcome instead of an ambiguous log sentence. Complete the typed event.

lessons.title: Consume Logs
lessons.instruction: Decode and validate an event before performing side effects. A valid log is acknowledged; malformed JSON or a missing event type is dead-lettered instead of retried forever. Fix the valid payload.

lessons.title: Schema
lessons.instruction: Additive schema changes are easiest to roll out when consumers tolerate missing and unknown fields. Decode the older payload and supply the new field's backward-compatible default.

lessons.title: Nodes and Clusters
lessons.instruction: A RabbitMQ cluster shares broker topology, while queue replication and consumer count are separate choices. Model three broker nodes, three queue replicas, and six consumers.

lessons.title: Backpressure
lessons.instruction: Backpressure bounds in-flight work instead of allowing producers to create an unlimited backlog. Give the local work queue a capacity of two.

lessons.title: Healthy Queues Are Empty
lessons.instruction: A near-empty queue can indicate balanced flow, but queue depth alone is not a health check. Compare publish and delivery rates plus message age to distinguish flowing traffic from a growing backlog.

lessons.title: Prefetch
lessons.instruction: Consumer prefetch caps unacknowledged deliveries and trades throughput against fairness. Process five deliveries in batches no larger than two.

lessons.title: Quorum Queues
lessons.instruction: Quorum queues replicate data with Raft and need a majority of members available. Compute the majority required by three-member and five-member groups.
